title: RBAC
summary: Roles, ClusterRoles and their bindings, the default roles, ServiceAccounts, and checking access with kubectl auth can-i.

blocks.text: At the Port of Kube, staff carry badges. A **badge card** (Role) lists what its holder may do in one company yard (namespace); a port-wide card (ClusterRole) covers the whole port. Handing a card to someone takes an **issuing slip** (RoleBinding, or ClusterRoleBinding port-wide). Cards only add powers: no card ever says "forbidden". The front desk (`kube-apiserver`) checks badges only when RBAC is listed in its `--authorization-mode`.
RBAC lives in the `rbac.authorization.k8s.io` API group. It defines four kinds: two hold permissions (roles) and two hand those permissions to someone (bindings).

steps.text: A **Role** lists rules: which verbs are allowed on which resources, within one namespace.
A **RoleBinding** grants a Role's permissions to subjects: users, groups or ServiceAccounts.
Permissions only add up; there are no deny rules. ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding work the same way cluster-wide.

rows: Define permissions on cluster-scoped resources (nodes), non-resource URLs (`/healthz`), or namespaced resources reused in many or all namespaces
Grant a Role, or a ClusterRole, inside the binding's namespace
Grant a ClusterRole across every namespace

items: Permissions only **add up**. There are no deny rules.
The API server enables RBAC when `--authorization-mode` includes `RBAC` (for example `--authorization-mode=...,RBAC`), or via an `--authorization-config` file listing the RBAC authorizer.

blocks.text: Each line on a badge card names three things: which department of forms (API group, `""` for the core one), which items by their filing name (`pods`), and which actions (verbs) are allowed. Sub-items like a bay's logbook (`pods/log`) get a slash. A star (`*`) means everything, even items invented next year, so careful harbormasters write explicit lists instead. A card can also name specific objects with `resourceNames`.
Each rule names the API groups, the resources (by the name used in the API URL, such as `pods`) and the verbs it allows.

apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  namespace: <namespace>
  name: <role-name>
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]          # "" = core API group
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]

items: **Subresources** use a slash: `pods/log`, `pods/status`.
`resourceNames` limits a rule to named objects. It can't restrict `deletecollection` or top-level `create`.
`*` is a wildcard for resources, apiGroups and verbs. It also matches resources added later, so prefer explicit lists (least privilege).
`nonResourceURLs` (such as `/healthz`) only take effect in a ClusterRole bound with a ClusterRoleBinding.

blocks.text: An issuing slip (binding) has two parts: the people receiving the badge (subjects: users, groups or robot crew ServiceAccounts) and exactly one card it points to (`roleRef`). Point a yard slip at a port-wide card and it only works in that yard, so common cards are written once and reused. Once printed, the card reference can't change; tear up the slip and issue a new one. Names starting `system:` are reserved for the port itself.
A binding has a list of **subjects** and one **roleRef**. Subjects are users, groups or ServiceAccounts.

kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: <binding-name>
  namespace: <namespace>
subjects:
- kind: User
  name: <user>             # case sensitive
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: <sa-name>
  namespace: <sa-namespace>
roleRef:
  kind: ClusterRole          # Role or ClusterRole
  name: <role-name>
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io

items: A RoleBinding that points at a ClusterRole grants those rights **only in the binding's namespace**. This lets you define common roles once and reuse them.
`roleRef` is **immutable**. To change it, delete the binding and create a new one (`kubectl auth reconcile` can do this for you).
ServiceAccount usernames look like `system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>` (singular). Their groups use `system:serviceaccounts:<namespace>` (plural).
The `system:` prefix is reserved for Kubernetes. Don't give users or groups names that start with it.

blocks.text: The front desk keeps four ready-made port-wide cards for people, and restocks any missing permissions every time it opens (auto-reconciliation). **cluster-admin** opens every door. **admin** runs a yard, badges included. **edit** moves cargo but can't touch badges. **view** only looks, and never inside sealed envelopes (Secrets). The last three are meant to be issued yard by yard. You can't print a card granting more than you hold, unless you have the `escalate` verb.
The API server creates default ClusterRoles and bindings and re-adds missing permissions to them at every start-up (auto-reconciliation). Four are meant for people:

rows: Any action on any resource. Bound to the `system:masters` group by default. In a RoleBinding: full control of that namespace.
Read/write most namespace objects, including Roles and RoleBindings. No write access to ResourceQuota or the namespace itself.
Read/write most namespace objects, but cannot view or change Roles or RoleBindings. Can read Secrets and run Pods as any ServiceAccount in the namespace.
Read-only on most namespace objects. Cannot see Roles, RoleBindings or **Secrets**.

items: admin, edit and view are intended to be granted per namespace with a RoleBinding.
They are aggregated: a ClusterRole labelled `rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-edit: "true"` (or `-admin`, `-view`) has its rules merged in.
You can only create a role containing permissions you already hold, unless you have the `escalate` verb. Binding a role needs those permissions or the `bind` verb.

blocks.text: Rather than drafting cards by hand, radio the front desk (`kubectl`) and have them printed on the spot: `kubectl create role` for a yard card, `kubectl create rolebinding` to issue a card in one yard, `kubectl create clusterrolebinding` to issue one port-wide. A favourite shortcut: issue the ready-made **view** card to one robot crew member with `--serviceaccount=<namespace>:<name>`, and you never have to write a new card at all.

kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get --verb=list --verb=watch --resource=pods
kubectl create role foo --verb=get,list,watch --resource=replicasets.apps
kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get --resource=pods --resource-name=<pod>
kubectl create clusterrole pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods

kubectl create rolebinding bob-admin-binding --clusterrole=admin --user=bob --namespace=acme
kubectl create rolebinding myapp-view-binding --clusterrole=view \
  --serviceaccount=acme:myapp --namespace=acme
kubectl create clusterrolebinding root-cluster-admin-binding \
  --clusterrole=cluster-admin --user=root

items: `--resource=<resource>.<group>` sets the API group (for example `replicasets.apps`).
`--serviceaccount` takes `<namespace>:<name>`. `--group` binds a group such as `system:serviceaccounts:<namespace>` (all ServiceAccounts in that namespace).
`kubectl create clusterrolebinding` grants a ClusterRole across all namespaces; `kubectl create rolebinding` grants it in one.

blocks.text: Read-only access for one app's ServiceAccount, straight from the docs: `kubectl create rolebinding my-sa-view --clusterrole=view --serviceaccount=my-namespace:my-sa --namespace=my-namespace`. Reusing a default ClusterRole saves writing a Role.

Robot crew members wear badges too (ServiceAccounts), and each belongs to one yard. Every yard comes with a robot badge named `default`; throw it away and the office prints a new one. Out of the box it opens almost nothing beyond the directory of forms (API discovery). A bay that names no badge gets `default`; set `spec.serviceAccountName` to pick another. Its pass code is short-lived and refreshed automatically. To work in another yard, issue the card in that target yard.

items: A ServiceAccount is a **namespaced**, non-human identity for workloads and automation. User accounts, by contrast, are not API objects.
Every namespace gets a `default` ServiceAccount. If you delete it, the control plane recreates it.
With RBAC, the default ServiceAccount has **no permissions** beyond API discovery.
A Pod with no ServiceAccount specified gets the namespace's `default` one. Set `spec.serviceAccountName` to use another.
Since v1.22 the Pod gets a short-lived, auto-rotating token from the TokenRequest API, mounted as a projected volume. Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` to stop that.
To let a ServiceAccount act in another namespace, create the Role and RoleBinding in the **target** namespace and name the ServiceAccount as subject.

sections.heading: Checking access with kubectl auth can-i

blocks.text: The front desk starts from "no": some checkpoint must say yes. Several checkpoints (authorization modes) are asked in order, and the first clear yes or no wins; a refusal comes back as **403**. Before trying a job, ask the desk yourself with `kubectl auth can-i`, even on someone else's behalf with `--as`. Careful: a card that lets you list sealed envelopes (Secrets) lets you read what's inside, because `get`, `list` and `watch` return everything.

Authorization is **deny by default**: some authorizer must allow the request. With several modes (e.g. `--authorization-mode=Node,RBAC,Webhook`) they are checked in order; the first allow or deny wins. A denied request gets HTTP **403**.

kubectl auth can-i create deployments --namespace dev
kubectl auth can-i list secrets --namespace dev --as dave
kubectl auth can-i list pods --namespace target \
  --as system:serviceaccount:dev:dev-sa
`get`, `list` and `watch` all return full objects. Granting `list` on Secrets reveals their data.

flashcards.back: Role: permissions within one namespace. ClusterRole: not namespaced; for cluster-scoped resources, non-resource URLs, or namespaced resources across namespaces.

flashcards.front: Can RBAC express a deny rule?
What happens when a RoleBinding references a ClusterRole?
flashcards.back: The ClusterRole's permissions apply only inside the RoleBinding's namespace.

flashcards.front: How do you change the roleRef of an existing binding?
flashcards.back: You can't edit it (immutable). Delete the binding and recreate it, or use kubectl auth reconcile.

flashcards.front: What apiGroups value means the core group (pods, services, secrets)?
How do you write the Pod logs subresource in a rule?
Group that contains all ServiceAccounts in one namespace?
Which default role can read/write most objects but NOT Roles/RoleBindings?
Which default role cannot read Secrets?
flashcards.back: view (reading Secrets could expose ServiceAccount credentials).

flashcards.front: Which group is bound to cluster-admin by default?
Pod spec field to choose a ServiceAccount?
flashcards.back: spec.serviceAccountName (and automountServiceAccountToken: false disables token injection).

flashcards.front: Check whether ServiceAccount dev-sa in namespace dev can list pods in namespace target?
flashcards.back: kubectl auth can-i list pods --namespace target --as system:serviceaccount:dev:dev-sa

questions.stem: A user must read Pods only in namespace `dev`. Which pair of objects is the minimal fit?

options.text: A Role in dev plus a RoleBinding in dev
options.explanation: A Role scopes permissions to one namespace and a RoleBinding grants them there.
A ClusterRoleBinding grants access in every namespace.

options.text: A Role in dev plus a ClusterRoleBinding
options.explanation: A ClusterRoleBinding grants access cluster-wide; to grant a role in just one namespace you use a RoleBinding.
A ServiceAccount is an identity; it carries no permissions by itself.

questions.stem: A RoleBinding in namespace `development` references the ClusterRole `secret-reader`. Where can the subject read Secrets?

options.explanation: The binding's namespace limits where the ClusterRole's permissions apply.
That would need a ClusterRoleBinding.

options.text: Nowhere; a RoleBinding cannot reference a ClusterRole
options.explanation: RoleBindings may reference ClusterRoles.
The binding namespace, not kube-system, decides.

questions.stem: True or false: You can add a rule to a Role that explicitly denies `delete` on Secrets.

options.explanation: RBAC has no deny rules.
Correct. Permissions are purely additive; there are no deny rules.

questions.stem: You try to edit an existing RoleBinding so its `roleRef` points to a different Role. What happens?

options.text: You get a validation error; you must delete and recreate the binding
options.explanation: roleRef is immutable after creation.

options.text: The binding updates and keeps its subjects
options.explanation: Changing roleRef is rejected.

options.text: The old Role is renamed to match
options.explanation: Roles are not renamed by bindings.

options.text: The API server creates a second binding automatically
options.explanation: It does not; kubectl auth reconcile can delete and recreate for you, but a plain edit fails.

questions.stem: Which command creates a Role in namespace `acme` that lets subjects get, list and watch ReplicaSets?

options.explanation: `<resource>.<group>` sets the apps API group.
This creates a cluster-scoped ClusterRole, not a Role in acme.
This binds the view role; it does not create a Role.

options.text: kubectl auth can-i list replicasets --namespace acme
options.explanation: This only checks access; it creates nothing.

questions.stem: Which statements about the default `view` ClusterRole are correct? Select 2.

options.text: It is intended to be granted within a namespace using a RoleBinding
options.explanation: admin, edit and view are meant for per-namespace grants.
Reading Secrets could expose ServiceAccount credentials.

options.text: It can list Roles and RoleBindings
options.explanation: view does not allow viewing roles or role bindings.
view is read-only.

questions.stem: Which default ClusterRole lets a namespace owner create Roles and RoleBindings in that namespace, but not modify its ResourceQuota?

options.explanation: admin includes role and role binding management but no write on resource quota or the namespace.
edit cannot view or modify roles or role bindings.
view is read-only.
cluster-admin can do anything, including quotas.

questions.stem: Which subject grants a role to **all** ServiceAccounts in namespace `qa`?

options.explanation: The plural prefix names the ServiceAccount group of that namespace.
The singular prefix is for one ServiceAccount username and needs a name after the namespace.

options.text: kind: ServiceAccount, name: default, namespace: qa
options.explanation: That is only the default ServiceAccount.
That is every authenticated user cluster-wide.

questions.stem: How do you check whether user `dave` can list Secrets in namespace `dev`?

options.text: kubectl auth can-i list secrets --namespace dev --as dave
options.explanation: --as impersonates the user for the check.

options.text: kubectl auth can-i list secrets --namespace dev
options.explanation: Without --as this checks the current user, not dave.
auth reconcile applies RBAC manifests.
This shows one binding, not the effective decision.

questions.stem: True or false: In a cluster with RBAC, a namespace's `default` ServiceAccount can list Pods in its namespace out of the box.

options.explanation: The default ServiceAccount gets only API discovery permissions.
Correct. It has no permissions beyond API discovery until you bind a role.

questions.stem: A Pod in namespace `dev` uses ServiceAccount `reporter` and must list Jobs in namespace `maintenance`. Where do you create the RoleBinding?

options.text: In maintenance, with the dev/reporter ServiceAccount as subject
options.explanation: Bind the Role in the namespace that holds the resources.
A RoleBinding in dev only grants access in dev.

options.text: Nowhere; ServiceAccounts cannot act across namespaces
options.explanation: RBAC allows cross-namespace access for ServiceAccounts.
That only controls token mounting.

questions.stem: Which HTTP request / RBAC verb pairs are correct? Select 3.

options.explanation: POST maps to create.
GET of a collection maps to list.
DELETE of a collection maps to deletecollection.
PUT maps to update; PATCH maps to patch.

questions.stem: The API server runs with `--authorization-mode=Node,RBAC`. The Node authorizer has no opinion on a request and RBAC has no matching rule. What is the result?

options.explanation: If every module has no opinion the request is denied.

options.text: Allowed because no rule denies it
options.explanation: Authorization is deny by default.

options.text: Passed to admission control to decide
options.explanation: Admission runs only after authorization allows.
There is no such fallback.

questions.stem: True or false: A user who cannot list Secrets cluster-wide can still create a ClusterRole granting that permission, as long as they may create ClusterRoles.

options.explanation: Escalation prevention blocks this unless they have the escalate verb.
Correct. They need the permission themselves or the `escalate` verb on clusterroles.
